activity_context.topic_title: Properties of Definite Integrals Involving the Limits of Integration

feedback.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{3}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factor out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)+3x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x+3{\int }_{0}^{3}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2+3\cdot \frac{1}{2}\cdot {x}^{2}\,{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-2+\frac{3}{2}({3}^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =-2+\frac{3}{2}\cdot 9 \\  & =-2+\frac{27}{2} \\  & =\frac{23}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
